I've been a loyal customer since T-Mobile launched its T-Mobile ONE plan back in 2016. I had a military discount during my time with T-Mobile, but even with that discount, the price hikes pushed my monthly bill to $113. I decided I'd had enough and started looking for cheaper alternatives. With this year's iPhone 18 Pro from Apple costing at least $100 more, I figured trimming my phone bill could help offset the cost of upgrading. So, I started shopping for an MVNO.

What is an MVNO?

MVNO stands for "Mobile Virtual Network Operator." Put simply, an MVNO is a wireless carrier that doesn't own its own nationwide cellular network. Instead, it buys network access from major carriers like AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon, and resells that service to its own customers. Think of them as middlemen for wireless service.

This means switching to an MVNO doesn't necessarily mean giving up your current network. For example, Mint Mobile uses T-Mobile's network, Visible uses Verizon's, and US Mobile lets you choose which of the three major networks you want to use. I'll be focusing on these three MVNOs in this article because they are primarily what I was comparing before leaving T-Mobile, but there are plenty of other options out there.

Simply put, MVNOs offer another way to purchase cellular service without going directly to the company that owns the network.

Why are MVNOs cheaper, and what are the catches?

If MVNOs can use the same networks as AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon, how can they charge so much less? The short answer is that MVNOs don't bear the full cost of operating a nationwide wireless network. They don't have to build and maintain their own networks, many operate primarily online without physical store locations, and they tend to have fewer employees. The savings can then be passed on to customers in the form of lower monthly bills.

MVNO plans also tend to be simpler, with fewer of the "perks" and extras that are common with traditional major carriers. Depending on the carrier and plan, you might not get free streaming services or other perks designed to keep you around. But if you really want those "free" perks, you can often pay for them yourself and still come out ahead with the savings from an MVNO.

That was certainly the case for me. I always looked forward to the free MLB.TV subscription that came with T-Mobile and used it every season, but I never watched Netflix, so the "free Netflix" perk was a complete waste for me. Even if I wanted Netflix plus MLB.TV, I could subscribe to those services myself and still come out ahead after accounting for the savings from switching carriers. At the end of the day, my main goal was finding reliable, affordable cellular service. I don't need a bunch of extras from T-Mobile just to use my phone.

The "catches" may not be worse service, but rather you're buying less. What exactly you give up depends on the MVNO and plan you choose. Video streaming might be limited in resolution, the amount of high-speed or premium data may differ, and network prioritization can vary. I have extremely fast Wi-Fi at home and rarely go to "packed" places like concerts or ballgames, so network prioritization isn't that important for my daily use. But I do travel internationally from time to time, so international data is an important consideration. Some MVNOs include international data and texting, while others charge extra or have more limited coverage outside the US.

There are also some less obvious differences, particularly when buying a new iPhone. If you choose an MVNO as your carrier, Apple Card installments and the iPhone Upgrade Program aren't available. To use those options, you're limited to AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon. That means if you want to buy your iPhone directly from Apple, you typically have to purchase it outright. Major carriers can also offer large trade-in credits and other promotions that generally aren't available through MVNOs. Apple Watch support isn't universally available either, so if you're using a cellular Apple Watch, that's something to keep in mind.

Finally, most MVNOs rely more heavily on phone and chat support rather than offering in-person help at physical retail stores. I'm comfortable with technology, and honestly, I have no desire to make a special trip to a store and wait in line for assistance. In my experience, the people at the stores often end up making the same phone call to the same support center and putting you on hold together anyway, so this isn't a dealbreaker for me.

Most importantly, these aren't inherent limitations of MVNOs—it depends on the carrier and plan. So it's worth looking carefully at what you're actually getting before making the switch.

Three MVNOs worth considering

Once I decided to leave T-Mobile, I started looking at alternatives. The postpaid plans from Verizon and AT&T were both still more expensive than what I was already paying, so I ruled out the other two major carriers right away. I narrowed my focus to US Mobile, Mint Mobile, and Visible. Each of these three had something I liked, and all three could significantly reduce my monthly bill while still using a major carrier's network.

US Mobile may be the most flexible of the three, and it was ultimately the carrier I switched to from T-Mobile. That doesn't necessarily mean it's the best fit for you, or even that it's the best MVNO of the three—it's just what happened to work best for me.

Actually, US Mobile wasn't my first choice initially. I hadn't even heard of the company before. But the more I looked into its service, the more impressed I became. Here's why: US Mobile has coverage on all three nationwide networks, letting customers choose the one that works best for them. It also offers a Multi-Network add-on feature that lets you have two networks active on the same iPhone (the additional network stays running in the background), so when coverage on your primary network is poor or the signal is weak, your iPhone can automatically switch to the secondary network (US Mobile officially says "when coverage is lower"). Using this feature requires enabling "Allow Cellular Data Switching" in your iPhone's Cellular Data settings. This feature is an extra cost with US Mobile—I didn't need it myself, but it's nice to have the option.

Since I had just moved, I was curious how Verizon's coverage near my new home compared to T-Mobile's, so I decided to test both networks. I set up my wife's iPhone on US Mobile's Light Speed network (which uses T-Mobile's) and put my own phone on Warp (which uses Verizon's), so we could compare coverage ourselves. The test results showed Verizon was noticeably better in our area, so switching to US Mobile was a win-win: better coverage and a significantly lower monthly bill.

Mint Mobile was actually my first choice because it's owned by T-Mobile, meaning I could keep using the same network I was already on while paying a lot less. What I didn't like was that it doesn't include international data. My wife and I enjoy cruises—travel is a part of our lifestyle—so having cellular data outside the US is important. Mint does offer international data services, but it costs extra and would eat into much of the savings. I also didn't like that taxes and fees are calculated separately.

Visible is similarly straightforward, but it only uses Verizon's network. What gave me the most pause with Visible was Verizon's coverage in my area. I'd been a T-Mobile customer for nearly a decade and knew exactly what T-Mobile's network looked like, but I had no idea what to expect from Verizon's coverage. That was the only reason I didn't immediately choose Visible over US Mobile—the latter let me try Verizon's network first, with T-Mobile and AT&T as backups. Visible's top-tier unlimited data plan also includes free cellular Apple Watch service, which is another appealing selling point. (US Mobile's top-tier plan on Warp, which uses Verizon's network, offers the same perk.)

What you need to switch

Switching to an MVNO was easier than I expected. My wife and I kept our existing iPhones, and it took about ten minutes to transfer both lines from T-Mobile to US Mobile. I didn't even have to get off the couch. You'll need an unlocked, compatible iPhone (or Android phone, though I'm focusing on iPhone here), along with some information from your current carrier. If you want to keep your existing phone number, be sure to wait until the number has transferred before canceling your old service.

Here's what you need to make the switch:

  • Your current carrier's account number
  • Transfer PIN
  • An unlocked, compatible iPhone
  • A new eSIM
  • A little patience

I prepaid for a full year of two unlimited data plans from US Mobile to make the switch. My wife doesn't use a cellular Apple Watch and doesn't mind lower video quality, so she chose US Mobile's Unlimited Starter plan, which costs $100 less than the Unlimited Premium plan I chose. Both lines plus the Apple Watch plan came to just $500 for the year, compared to $1,356 a year for two lines with no Apple Watch service on T-Mobile. (Again, that price already includes the military discount!)

Getting the transfer PIN from T-Mobile was straightforward—I expected it to be buried somewhere or overly complicated, but it wasn't at all. Here are instructions for Verizon and AT&T.

After connecting my iPhone to Wi-Fi, US Mobile sent me an email with the eSIM, and installation was as simple as tapping a button in the email and following the on-screen instructions. My wife's iPhone followed the same process. The only extra step was pairing my Apple Watch, which was easily handled through US Mobile's app.

Why I'm sticking with an MVNO

Same coverage, a lot cheaper: What I've given up is absolutely worth the money I've saved. I have extremely fast Wi-Fi at home, so cellular data isn't that critical for me (though in speed tests, US Mobile was just as fast as T-Mobile). What matters most is having a strong, reliable cellular signal when I'm away from Wi-Fi, especially for sending and receiving texts and making calls.

No long-term contracts: Most carriers have moved away from traditional service contracts and toward device installment plans, which can effectively lock you in until the device is paid off. I've always preferred buying my iPhones directly from Apple because I want the freedom of an unlocked device, but US Mobile, Mint, and Visible all let you go without a contract, which I think is great.

Easy to switch: Most MVNOs let you pay month to month without a long-term commitment. If one carrier has a promotion this month and another is cheaper next month, switching is easy and painless. Prepaid accounts also don't require a credit check, meaning your credit score won't take a hit every time a carrier pulls your credit, unlike with postpaid accounts, and you won't be turned away due to poor credit. My credit is fine, but if I decided to switch from T-Mobile to Verizon and was hit with a hard inquiry, I'd still rather not take that hit.

Top-rated comment from Richard Lewis (Rich)

Switching from AT&T to Mint Mobile a few years ago was one of the smartest tech decisions I've ever made.

Save more by prepaying for a year: The tradeoff for flexibility is that if you're willing to pay for a full year of service upfront, you can save even more. Most MVNOs offer significant discounts on annual plans, so you're trading a little flexibility to switch at any time for a lower overall price.

No surprise charges: As I mentioned earlier, my wife and I enjoy cruises. If you've ever forgotten to put your iPhone in airplane mode on a ship and it automatically connected to the ship's cellular network, you know you can easily end up with a shocking bill. With a prepaid plan, I don't have to worry about accidentally racking up massive roaming charges. If international roaming isn't included, my phone simply won't connect to foreign networks and bill me. US Mobile's plans also include taxes and fees, so the listed price is exactly what you pay.

Switching to an MVNO is about more than just finding the cheapest service—it's about buying the service I need without paying for a bunch of things I don't. So far, I haven't felt like I'm missing out on anything that matters to me (though I do genuinely miss that free MLB.TV subscription). In fact, I now have an extra Apple Watch line I didn't have before, and my monthly bill is even lower. My iPhone is the same, my number is the same, coverage in my area is actually better on US Mobile's Warp (Verizon) network, and I've kept the freedom to switch again if I find a better option down the road.

Your priorities may be different from mine, and an MVNO isn't necessarily the right choice for everyone. But if you're paying a lot for your current cellular service and haven't considered an MVNO, it's worth looking into. You might find you sacrifice less than you think.
